$schema_note: User-visible product improvements, newest first. Feeds the pipeline's What's-new card and the homepage footer's latest-improvement stamp — one source, both surfaces (the homepage must match the real site). Keep entries honest, dated, and user-phrased; trim to ~12.

entries.title: Verification sweep — every internal link checked, and a scope contradiction caught
entries.blurb: A full crawl of the public site: all 41 pages (every metro brief, all 14 sector tabs, every marketing page) return 200, and all 53 unique internal links resolve — no dead ends. The sweep also caught the homepage contradicting itself: the pulse board called its 18 tiles '18 covered markets' while the same page said '15 markets, deliberately.' Tiles are per jurisdiction — DC, Prince George's, Montgomery and Northern Virginia are four tiles inside one DMV-core market — so the board now reads '18 jurisdiction tiles across 15 covered markets,' both numbers derived. Three tests pin the counts so a future market can't reopen the gap.

entries.title: Which assumption moved the IRR — the assumption bridge
entries.blurb: Re-run a deal with a lower price and a tighter exit cap and the return jumps, but nothing used to say which change did the work. It can't be answered one-at-a-time either: cutting price is worth more after the cap tightens than before it, so the answer depends on the order. The bridge uses Shapley values over the changed assumptions instead — order-independent, exact to six changed fields and sampled above that, with the waterfall's bars summing to the headline move exactly. Every model run is snapshotted as a version, so the comparison is always available.

entries.title: Two brokers, one asset — the BOV reconciler
entries.blurb: JLL says $71.5M, Eastdil says $65M, and finding where the $6.5M lives used to take an afternoon in Excel. Upload both and the gap decomposes into Year-1 NOI, cap rate and capex treatment, using the symmetric split so the answer doesn't depend on which factor you apply first. Anything the identity can't explain is shown as unexplained rather than smoothed away, a cap rate backed out of a value and an NOI is labelled derived rather than stated, and each broker's price then runs through your own model so you see the levered IRR each one actually implies.

entries.title: Rent rolls in, and an Excel model whose formulas are alive
entries.blurb: Broker rent rolls are never the same twice — the header is rarely row 1, the columns never match, and rent is monthly on one file and annual on the next. Upload a CSV or XLSX, correct whatever the column mapper missed (it remembers, so the next file from the same broker is one click), and get WALT weighted by both SF and rent, the rollover schedule, mark-to-market and the rollover cost forecast. Then download a four-tab workbook that is a real model: change the exit cap on the Assumptions tab and the IRR recalculates. CI proves it, recalculating the generated file in LibreOffice and asserting its IRR matches the app's to four decimals.

entries.title: Exit cap and rent growth, checked against the submarket
entries.blurb: The two assumptions that swing returns most are usually just typed in, and nothing checks them — a deal underwritten to 4% rent growth in a market with 18 months of supply under construction is a bad deal that screens well. Build a submarket from your own market export and those assumptions get measured against what it actually did: months of supply, trailing rent CAGR on a consistent basis, trough vacancy. Four data traps are handled by name — data-center campuses excluded by a persistent rule, rent-basis changes breaking the trend line instead of being averaged through, a pipeline that doesn't tie reconciled with the delta shown, and round-number placeholders flagged for review. Overriding a warning is normal; it needs a one-line reason, and the reason lands in the memo.

entries.title: The whole board — every market and asset class in one grid
entries.blurb: The market page gains a coverage grid: 18 metro entries down, office/industrial/multifamily/retail across, each cell that market's vacancy read. Shading is computed within each column, so office compares to office — DC industrial at 7.4% shades tight while DC retail at 6.3% shades loose, because those are different worlds. 66 of the 72 cells carry a sourced figure; the other 6 render as dashed gaps that say why rather than implying coverage that isn't there. Bands stay bands throughout.

entries.title: Deal pages: benchmark units follow the metric, and vacancy rows get pack positions
entries.blurb: The vs-market panel on deal pages printed every benchmark with a dollar sign — including percent figures, so an office deal read 'office vacancy: $17.7–$22.3'. Units now follow the metric: vacancy, cap rates, and the 30-yr PMMS print as percents, rents as $/SF, sales and listing counts plain, medians and FMRs keep their dollars — locked in by unit tests. And each vacancy row now carries the metro's rank across the covered markets, from the same shared builder as the rankings, the briefs, and the sample screen — the deal page is the fourth surface that can never disagree.

entries.title: The changelog becomes a tour — every improvement links to where it landed
entries.blurb: What's-new now shows the full log grouped by ship day with a running count (19 improvements landed on Aug 25 alone), a momentum line derived from the log itself, and a 'See it live' link on every entry — the log names where in the app each change lives, so the page doubles as a guided tour. The covered-markets band now runs here too, same as /why and /demo.

entries.title: The sample screen says where Philadelphia sits in the pack
entries.blurb: The demo's asset-type line now carries pack positions from the same shared ranking builder as the market page: Philadelphia office #10 of 18, industrial #17 of 17 — the wide 10.3–15.5% two-tracker band honestly lands it loosest — and multifamily #6 of 18. Retail carries no rank because its numeric level is held open, so no position is invented. Ranks run tightest first, and all three surfaces (sample screen, metro briefs, rankings) derive from one function.

entries.title: The cap hunt continues — two more templated catches, real Yardi texture for Baltimore
entries.blurb: The Baltimore and Richmond multifamily cap fields stay honestly null after another sweep: the loan-store '5.6% across all classes' boilerplate turned up twice more — once spliced into a digest under Berkadia's Q1 framing (the fingerprint phrase gave it away; eighth sighting), once printed at the state level for all of Virginia (one number claiming to price every market in a state is self-refuting; ninth). A separate unattributed 'averaging 8.5–9%' claim was rejected for naming no research house. What did survive the filter: Yardi Matrix's March 2026 Baltimore print — 94.8% occupancy for stabilized assets (construct declared, not comparable to the vacancy band), $1,744/mo average advertised asking, Q1 absorption 219 units against 260 delivered.

entries.title: Rank chips on every brief — each sector read says where it sits in the pack
entries.blurb: Every metro brief's asset-type rows now carry a rank chip — Northern Virginia industrial reads #1 of 17, DC office #13 of 18 — computed from the same shared leaderboard builder as the rankings table and the homepage lens, so the three surfaces can never disagree. Chips only appear where a numeric vacancy ranks; a metro whose level is held open gets no invented position. Each chip clicks through to the full cross-metro ranking.

entries.title: The sector lens — the board now names the tightest market per asset class
entries.blurb: Under the pulse board, four chips carry the tightest covered market on file for office, industrial, multifamily, and retail — today that's four different metros (Hampton Roads office, Northern Virginia industrial, New York multifamily, Boston retail), each with its vacancy band kept as a band and a count of how many markets are ranked. Every chip opens the full cross-metro ranking, and both surfaces derive from the same shared leaderboard builder, so the homepage can never drift from the market page.

entries.title: Sector leaderboards — every covered market ranked, one asset class at a time
entries.blurb: The market page's asset-class explorer now flips the metro tiles the other way: pick office, industrial, multifamily, or retail and see every covered market with a numeric read ranked tightest to loosest — vacancy bands kept as bands (a spread is never averaged into one printed number), asking $/SF and cap ranges where sourced, a source link on every row. Metros whose level is honestly held open are named under the table, never silently dropped.
